claim: The testis has the largest number of tissue specific genes, over twice as many as the cerebral cortex.
source: its transcriptome has by far the largest number of tissue specific genes (over twice as many as the 2nd ranked tissue the cerebral cortex – with which the testis shares an unusual similarity) (Djureinovic et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2005; Uhlén et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Djureinovic et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2005; Uhlén et al., 2015).

claim: The testis shares an unusual similarity with the cerebral cortex.
source: its transcriptome has by far the largest number of tissue specific genes (over twice as many as the 2nd ranked tissue the cerebral cortex – with which the testis shares an unusual similarity) (Djureinovic et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2005; Uhlén et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Djureinovic et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2005; Uhlén et al., 2015).

claim: The testis contains the only cells in the male body with sex chromosome inactivation.
source: it contains the only cells in the male body with sex chromosome inactivation (Yan and McCarrey, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yan and McCarrey, 2009.

claim: Meiotic cells undergo programed double strand break formation, homologous chromosome pairing, and recombination.
source: meiotic cells undergo programed double strand break formation, homologous chromosome pairing, and recombination
evidence: This is established knowledge about meiosis.

claim: Cells undergoing meiosis share transcripts through cytoplasmic bridges.
source: cells undergoing meiosis share transcripts through cytoplasmic bridges (Braun et al., 1989)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Braun et al., 1989.

claim: During spermiogenesis, the majority of histones are stripped away and replaced with protamines.
source: it features dramatic chromatin remodeling, when the majority of histones are stripped away during spermiogenesis and replaced with small, highly basic proteins known as protamines (Hammoud et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hammoud et al., 2009.

claim: Single cell expression profiles from enzymatic and mechanical dissociation methods showed excellent agreement (r = 0.95).
source: Single cell expression profiles from the two methods showed excellent agreement (r = 0.95), with no important differences in cell quality or ascertainment (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, showing correlation coefficient r = 0.95.

claim: The study generated 25,423 cell profiles from wild-type animals.
source: We performed scRNA-seq to generate 25,423 cell profiles isolated from total testis dissociations of 11 wild-type animals (WT1-WT11).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data generated.

claim: The study generated 31,400 single cell profiles from four different mutant mouse strains.
source: We added to this an additional 31,400 single cell profiles from four different mutant mouse strains exhibiting spermatogenesis defects: three mutants with known molecular mechanisms (knockouts of Mlh3, Hormad1, and Cul4a) as well as one knockin of a transgene (Cnp) that led to idiopathic infertility.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data generated.

claim: Mlh3-/- and Hormad1-/- mice exhibit complete early meiotic arrest and absence of spermatozoa.
source: Seminiferous tubules in Mlh3-/- and Hormad1-/- mice exhibited complete early meiotic arrest and absence of spermatozoa.
evidence: This is based on histological confirmation described in the manuscript.

claim: Cul4a-/- sections showed partial impairment of spermatogenesis with a significant decrease in number of post-meiotic cells and abnormal spermatids.
source: Cul4a-/- sections showed partial impairment of spermatogenesis, with a significant decrease in number of post-meiotic cells and abnormal spermatids.
evidence: This is based on histological confirmation described in the manuscript.

claim: Cnp mice displayed a clear defect in spermatogenesis with grossly reduced number of elongating spermatids.
source: Cnp mice displayed a clear defect in spermatogenesis; the number of elongating spermatids was grossly reduced to compared to wild-type, and the few elongating spermatids seen in the histology sections featured misshapen nuclear morphology and odd orientation within the disorganized tubules.
evidence: This is based on histological confirmation described in the manuscript.

claim: SDA was run on the post-QC final matrix with 50 components for 10,000 iterations.
source: SDA v1.1 (Hore, 2015; Hore et al., 2016) was then run on the post-QC final matrix with 50 components for 10,000 iterations to confirm convergence (although in practice the results are almost identical after just 1000 iterations).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the computational methods used.

claim: K-means clustering of single cell libraries resulted in 32 distinct clusters.
source: We visualized the resulting 32 distinct clusters in t-SNE space (Materials and methods, Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the clustering results, with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: The 32 clusters were resolved into 11 distinct subtypes of germ cells and four somatic cell populations.
source: Next, by inspecting the expression levels of known cell type markers and comparing to the FACS-sorted cells, we could resolve our 32 clusters into 11 distinct subtypes of germ cells and four somatic cell populations – Leydig cells, Sertoli cells, immune cells, and telocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of known cell type markers and comparison to FACS-sorted cells.

claim: Both Mlh3-/- and Hormad1-/- cells arrest at different stages of meiosis I.
source: Consistent with the known biology, we observed that both Mlh3-/- and Hormad1-/- cells arrest at different stages of meiosis I; mid-pachytene and leptotene/zygotene respectively.
evidence: This is based on analysis of cell locations in t-SNE space and is consistent with known biology.

claim: Cells from Mlh3-/- and Hormad1-/- animals showed higher rates of apoptosis compared to wild-type (2% vs 14.5%).
source: Cells from Mlh3-/- and Hormad1-/- animals showed higher rates of apoptosis compared to wild-type, Cul4a and Cnp (2% vs 14.5%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of mitochondrial gene expression as a marker of apoptosis.

claim: KIF5B is a Sertoli cell protein that provides more extensive coverage of the cell body than conventional markers TUBB and VIM.
source: Noteworthy is the identification of KIF5B as a Sertoli cell protein that provides more extensive coverage of the cell body than the conventional markers TUBB and VIM
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry validation shown in Figure 2.

claim: ABHD5 is a marker for the residual body in developing germ cells.
source: the identification of ABHD5 as a marker for the subcellular structure of developing germ cells known as the residual body
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry validation shown in Figure 2.

claim: SDA produces the most sparse model compared to NNMF, PCA, and ICA.
source: when compared to alternative commonly used methods for matrix factorisation (non-negative matrix factorization, NNMF; principal component analysis, PCA; independent component analysis, ICA), SDA produced the most sparse model (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of sparsity metrics shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Component 5 is highly and specifically enriched for GWAS hits of human recombination rate.
source: Strikingly, this component is highly enriched for GWAS hits of recombination rate in humans (Halldorsson et al., 2019). Of the 24 significant GWAS loci identified with confidently associated causal genes, more than half (13) rank within the top 300 genes of this component, and almost all (20) rank within the top 1300 genes (p=5.2×10−18, OR = 77.8 and p=2.4×10−20, OR = 70.1 respectively by Fisher's exact test [FET], Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test) comparing component genes to GWAS hits, with citation to Halldorsson et al., 2019.

claim: Zcwpw1 ranks 3rd in component 5, after Prdm9.
source: One striking candidate gene is Zcwpw1, which ranks 3rd, after Prdm9.
evidence: This is based on the gene loadings in component 5.

claim: ZCWPW1 contains two protein domains: CW and PWWP, known to bind H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 respectively.
source: This gene does not have a known function, but contains two protein domains: CW and PWWP, known to bind H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 respectively (He et al., 2010; Rona et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to He et al., 2010 and Rona et al., 2016.

claim: PRDM9 deposits both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 at sites it binds.
source: PRDM9 deposits both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 at sites it binds (Powers et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Powers et al., 2016.

claim: PRDM9's methyltransferase activity is essential for its role in double strand break positioning.
source: this methyltransferase activity is essential for its role in double strand break positioning (Diagouraga et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Diagouraga et al., 2018.

claim: Meiotic sex chromosome inactivation (MSCI) is observed from the start of pachytene.
source: As previously reported (Chen et al., 2018; Green et al., 2018; Lukassen et al., 2018) we observe MSCI from the start of pachytene (Figure 6A and Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of sex chromosome expression shown in Figure 6A, consistent with previous reports.

claim: No genes were confidently identified as escaping MSCI.
source: Although previous bulk RNA-seq studies suggested that some genes escape MSCI (da Cruz et al., 2016; Soumillon et al., 2013), we were unable to confidently identify any genes escaping MSCI.
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene expression data, contrasting with previous bulk RNA-seq studies.

claim: Previously identified 'escapees' of MSCI are actually expressed after MSCI, yet fully silenced within MSCI.
source: Moreover, our data indicate that previously identified 'escapees' are actually expressed after MSCI, yet fully silenced within MSCI (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Genetically haploid cells are predominantly phenotypically diploid with respect to sex chromosome transcription.
source: Here, we find that, with respect to sex chromosome transcription, the genetically haploid cells are predominantly phenotypically diploid (Figure 6A & B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) suggesting that cytoplasmic mRNA is efficiently shared
evidence: This is based on analysis of sex chromosome expression shown in Figure 6A & B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cytoplasmic mRNA is efficiently shared in post-meiotic cells.
source: suggesting that cytoplasmic mRNA is efficiently shared, consistent with studies of individual genes (Braun et al., 1989) and recent scRNA-seq reports (Chen et al., 2018; Green et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: De novo motif analysis identified 16 groups of matched motifs.
source: We compared the resulting motifs with known motifs from the HOCOMOCO database, resulting in 16 groups of matched motifs, including one group of identified de novo motifs not clearly associated with any known transcription factor, but most similar to the binding target of ATF1 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of promoter sequences and comparison to known motifs.

claim: Identified motifs include the binding targets of master regulators of spermatogenesis: Stra8, Mybl1, Rfx2, and Crem.
source: Although identified independently, the identified motifs include the binding targets of multiple master regulators of spermatogenesis: Stra8 (Kojima et al., 2019), Mybl1 (Bolcun-Filas et al., 2011), Rfx2 (Kistler et al., 2015), and Crem (Nantel and Sassone-Corsi, 1996).
evidence: This is based on comparison of de novo motifs to known transcription factor binding sites, with citations to relevant studies.

claim: The binding target of Spi1 (PU.1), a known master regulator of macrophage differentiation, was identified specifically in the macrophage component 11.
source: In addition, we identified the target of Spi1 (aka PU.1), a known master regulator of macrophage differentiation (Rosa et al., 2007), specifically in the macrophage component 11.
evidence: This is based on motif analysis and supported by a citation to Rosa et al., 2007.

claim: High and specific enrichment of ChIP-seq targets of STRA8, MYBL1, RFX2 and CREM validated the interpretation that covariation of expression within many components reflects shared transcriptional regulation.
source: High and specific enrichment of ChIP-seq targets of STRA8, MYBL1, RFX2 and CREM validated our interpretation - that covariation of expression of genes within many components reflects shared transcriptional regulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of overlap between component genes and ChIP-seq targets, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most pre-division motifs contain CpG dinucleotides.
source: Strikingly, many of the pre-division motifs as well as MLX/CREM contain CpG dinucleotides (Figure 7)
evidence: This is based on analysis of motif sequences shown in Figure 7.

claim: None of the post-division motifs contain CpGs, excepting one ATF like motif believed to be Crem-t.
source: None of the post-division motifs contain CpGs, excepting one ATF like motif that we believe is instead Crem-t (see below).
evidence: This is based on analysis of motif sequences.

claim: There is a major shift away from expression of genes whose promoters contain CpG islands following the meiotic divisions.
source: Indeed, we found an even stronger pattern of association simply using the count of CpG occurrences as a pseudo-motif (Figure 7B), indicating a major shift away from expression of genes whose promoters contain CpG islands, following the meiotic divisions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of CpG occurrence in promoters shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Component 38 is comprised largely of genes on the X chromosome and is restricted to Hormad1-/- cells.
source: We found one SDA component (38) with much higher gene loadings on the sex chromosomes than autosomes (Figure 9A, Figure 4—figure supplement 3C, Supplementary file 3), and with cell loadings that are specific to Hormad1-/-.
evidence: This is based on analysis of component gene loadings and cell scores shown in Figure 9A and Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Hormad1-/- cells not only fail to silence previously expressed sex-linked genes, but many previously unexpressed sex-linked genes obtain high expression.
source: We find that not only does Hormad1-/- fail to silence previously expressed sex-linked genes, but many previously unexpressed sex-linked genes such as Rhox2h obtain high expression (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene expression shown in Figure 9B.

claim: There is a very strong association between genes in component 38 and genes overexpressed in mice with mutations in either Hormad1 or Trip13.
source: We find a very strong association between genes in this component and genes overexpressed in mice which have mutations in either Hormad1 or Trip13 (p = 2.2×10−39, OR = 184 and p = 1.3×10−157, OR = 115, respectively by FET) (Ortega, 2016; Figure 4—figure supplement 3A&B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test) comparing component genes to genes overexpressed in mutants, with citation to Ortega, 2016.

claim: Component 25 is highly specific to Cul4a-/- cells.
source: We identified a single SDA component (25) that was highly specific to Cul4a-/- cells (Figure 9C and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of component cell scores shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Component 25 corresponds to dozens of genes that are overexpressed in Cul4a-/- mutants with GO enrichments related to spermatid development, motility and capacitation.
source: This component corresponds to dozens of genes that are overexpressed in Cul4a-/- mutants when compared to all other strains, with GO enrichments related to spermatid development, motility and capacitation.
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis and GO enrichment analysis of component 25 genes.

claim: No obvious transcriptional phenotype was found in Mlh3-/- cells by SDA analysis or by comparison of expression levels between hard-clustered wild-type and mutant cells.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to Hormad1-/-, we found no obvious transcriptional phenotype in Mlh3-/- cells either by SDA analysis or by comparison of expression levels between hard-clustered wild-type and mutant cells (other than differential expression of Mlh3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of SDA components and differential expression analysis.

claim: Six somatic components (3, 16, 49, 40, 26, and 32) show specific enrichment for Mlh3-/- and Hormad1-/- cell loadings compared to all other strains.
source: Despite the differences in cell composition or component loadings among mutant strains, we identified six somatic components (3, 16, 49, 40, 26, and 32) showing a specific enrichment for Mlh3-/- and Hormad1-/- cell loadings when compared to all other strains (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of component cell scores shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Hypothesis-free GO enrichment analysis of six components revealed a recurrence of amyloid related GO terms with qvalue <0.01.
source: Hypothesis-free GO enrichment analysis of these components (Materials and methods) revealed a recurrence of amyloid related GO terms with qvalue <0.01, with these terms being the highest enriched term in three components (26N, 49N, 16N, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis of component genes.

claim: Component 11 (macrophages) is specifically and strongly enriched for Alzheimer's disease risk genes identified in a recent GWAS.
source: To further evaluate the expression of Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related genes across all five mouse strains, we tested individual SDA components for enrichment of expression of AD risk genes identified in a recent GWAS, identifying component 11 (macrophages) as specifically and strongly enriched (p=1.3x10−11, OR=65.9 by FET, Figure 9D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test) comparing component genes to AD GWAS hits, shown in Figure 9D.

claim: APOE+ cells are found within the tubules of Mlh3-/- and Hormad1-/- but not wild-type.
source: Both Mlh3-/- and Hormad1-/- displayed interstitial cell with more intense staining of APOE, as well as a greater abundance of APOE+ cells. More surprisingly, we also found a rare population of APOE+ cells within the tubules of Mlh3-/- and Hormad1-/-, that was never observed in wild-type.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The frequency of intratubular APOE+ cells is significantly higher in Mlh3-/- (3.5%) and Hormad1-/- (5.6%) compared to wild-type (0%).
source: We screened 4959 tubule cross-sections to establish more precise estimates of APOE+ cell frequency in these three lines (Materials and methods). When compared to the frequency in wild-type tubules (0/2496 tubules), we see higher frequencies of intratubular APOE+ cells in Mlh3-/- (25/707 tubules, 3.5%, p<2.2×10−16) and Hormad1-/- (98/1756 tubules, 5.6%, p<2.2×10−16).
evidence: This is based on quantification of immunofluorescence staining and statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test).

claim: Intratubular APOE+ cells stained for F4/80, a well-established macrophage antigen.
source: These APOE+ intratubular cells stained for F4/80, a well-established macrophage antigen
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence co-staining shown in Figure 9E.

claim: In Mlh3-/- and Hormad1-/- mutants, immune cells can transit the blood-testis barrier and enter an area typically regarded as immune-privileged.
source: These APOE+ intratubular cells stained for F4/80, a well-established macrophage antigen, perhaps surprisingly, given that it suggests that in these mutants, immune cells can transit the blood-testis barrier and enter an area typically regarded as immune-privileged.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of F4/80+ macrophages within seminiferous tubules, which are normally immune-privileged.

claim: SDA imputation outperforms approaches using raw data for essentially all cells in the test data.
source: SDA imputation outperforms approaches using the raw data, for essentially all cells in the test data (Figure 5B&C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on cross-validation analysis shown in Figure 5B&C.

claim: SDA provides the most sparse representation while imputing equally well compared to other matrix factorizations and MAGIC.
source: While providing the most sparse representation (Figure 3C), SDA still imputes equally well, compared to other matrix factorizations and to MAGIC (van Dijk et al., 2018) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on comparison of imputation performance and sparsity metrics shown in Figure 3C and Figure 5C.

claim: Of 50 SDA components, six represent batch effects.
source: Overall, of 50 components, six represent batch effects, five are components with only a single cell, 13 are observed only in somatic cell types, 23 only in germ cells, and three components load on both somatic and germ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis and interpretation of SDA components.

claim: Of 50 SDA components, 13 are observed only in somatic cell types.
source: Overall, of 50 components, six represent batch effects, five are components with only a single cell, 13 are observed only in somatic cell types, 23 only in germ cells, and three components load on both somatic and germ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis and interpretation of SDA components.

claim: Of 50 SDA components, 23 are observed only in germ cells.
source: Overall, of 50 components, six represent batch effects, five are components with only a single cell, 13 are observed only in somatic cell types, 23 only in germ cells, and three components load on both somatic and germ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis and interpretation of SDA components.

claim: Pachytene gene regulation can be decomposed into five components (13, 39, 42, 47, and 48).
source: Here, we are able to decompose pachytene gene regulation into five components (13, 39, 42, 47, and 48).
evidence: This is based on SDA analysis identifying multiple components active during pachytene.

claim: Component 31 represents undifferentiated spermatogonia expressing Zbtb16 and Foxo1.
source: Component 31 represents undifferentiated spermatogonia expressing Zbtb16 (aka Plzf) (Buaas et al., 2004) and Foxo1 (Goertz et al., 2011)
evidence: This is based on analysis of component gene loadings and supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Component 50 splits undifferentiated spermatogonia into two subpopulations, one expressing Gfra1 and Glis3, and the other expressing Nanos3, Lin28a and Foxf1.
source: while component 50 splits these into two subpopulations one expressing, Gfra1 (He et al., 2007) and Glis3 (Kang et al., 2016), and the other Nanos3 (Suzuki et al., 2009), Lin28a (Zheng et al., 2009) and Foxf1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of component gene loadings shown in Figure 5D and supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Component 7 likely represents A1-4 spermatogonia expressing Glis2, Nanos1, Kit, and Stra8.
source: Component seven likely represents A1-4 spermatogonia expressing Glis2, Nanos1, Kit, and Stra8.
evidence: This is based on analysis of component gene loadings.

claim: Component 2 likely represents intermediate and type B spermatogonia, including Ctcfl, Pou4f1, and Esx1.
source: Component two includes Ctcfl, Pou4f1, and Esx1 - likely representing intermediate and type B spermatogonia
evidence: This is based on analysis of component gene loadings.

claim: Component 20 contains genes likely to be functional during meiotic divisions and perhaps afterwards.
source: Component 20 is particularly interesting, containing genes likely to be functional during meiotic divisions and perhaps afterwards.
evidence: This is based on analysis of component gene loadings and their known functions.

claim: Component 20 shows very strong enrichment of genes characterized by the presence of a DUF622 domain (18 in the top 88 genes).
source: It contains a number of genes known to be expressed in diplotene and/or key regulators of cell division, in addition to the Ssx family of genes (discussed further below) and also shows very strong enrichment of genes characterized by the presence of a DUF622 domain (18 in the top 88 genes) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of component gene loadings.

claim: Component 9 is very highly enriched for genes of the electron transport chain (p=7.4×10−53, OR = 104).
source: Another component (9) is most active at a similar time to 20, and is very highly enriched for genes of the electron transport chain (p=7.4×10−53, OR = 104, FET) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4E&F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test) of component gene loadings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4E&F.

claim: Round spermatid component 30 contains many genes associated with the acrosome.
source: Round spermatid component 30 contains many genes associated with the acrosome, an organelle which forms a nuclear cap containing hydrolytic enzymes used in fertilization (Ito and Toshimori, 2016) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of component gene loadings and supported by a citation to Ito and Toshimori, 2016.

claim: Lrrc34 protein is localized to the acrosome of round spermatids.
source: For one high loading gene, Lrrc34, we verified by immunofluorescence that the protein is indeed localized to the acrosome of round spermatids (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence validation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Component 35 is the most mysterious of all components detected.
source: Component 35, which is essentially concurrent to component 30 in pseudotime, is the most mysterious of all components that we detected.
evidence: This is a subjective assessment based on the lack of known functions for genes in this component.

claim: Dozens of protein-coding genes in component 35 are highly enriched in testis expression but have no known function.
source: Dozens of protein-coding genes in this component are highly enriched in testis expression but have no known function (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of component gene loadings and their annotations.

claim: Component 35 harbors a substantial number of genes with no apparent ortholog in humans.
source: This component also harbors a substantial number of genes with no apparent ortholog in humans.
evidence: This is based on analysis of component gene loadings and orthology information.

claim: Abhd5 (CGI-58) serves as an excellent marker of the residual body.
source: In addition, Abhd5 (aka CGI-58), a protein previously detected in testis lipid droplets (Wang et al., 2015), has high loadings specifically in these late components (17 and 18) and we show by immunofluorescence that it serves as an excellent marker of the residual body (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence validation shown in Figure 2B and supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Telocytes are identified based on coexpression of Cd34 and Pdgfra.
source: We also find a component representing an abundant somatic cell type expressing Tcf21 but not Acta2, described by Green et al. (2018) as an unknown mesenchymal celltype, which we identify as telocytes based on coexpression of Cd34 and Pdgfra (Kuroda et al., 2004; Marini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on analysis of component gene loadings and supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: In addition to previously reported markers Cd34 and Pdgfra, telocytes have highly specific expression markers including Dcn, Gsn, and Tcf21.
source: In addition to the previously reported markers Cd34 and Pdgfra, we find a number of even more highly specific expression markers for telocytes, including Dcn, Gsn, Tcf21 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of component gene loadings.

claim: The pseudotime-ordered set of 16,950 germ cells spans the entire ~34.5 day development process from Type A spermatogonia to mature spermatozoa.
source: Our our pseudotime-ordered set of 16,950 germ cells spans the entire ~34.5 day (Oakberg, 1957) development process from Type A spermatogonia to mature spermatozoa, suggesting a mean difference in developmental age between pseudotime-adjacent cells of 3 minutes.
evidence: This is based on pseudotime analysis and supported by a citation to Oakberg, 1957 for the duration of spermatogenesis.

claim: The estimated difference in the mean time of arrest of Hormad1-/- cells and Mlh3-/- cells is 12 days.
source: Although further work is needed to clarify the mapping of pseudotime to real time, that mapping estimates the difference in the mean time of arrest of Hormad1-/- cells and Mlh3-/- cells to be 12 days.
evidence: This is based on pseudotime analysis.

claim: Mlh3-/- animals possess cells that load on pachytene components 47, 42 and 39, while Hormad1-/- animals do not.
source: This difference is reflected in the SDA components as well; Mlh3-/- animals possess cells that load on pachytene components 47, 42 and 39, while Hormad1-/- animals do not.
evidence: This is based on analysis of component cell scores.

claim: HORMAD1 normally marks un-synapsed chromosomes.
source: HORMAD1 is a meiosis-specific protein that regulates chromosome recombination, synapsis, and segregation. HORMAD1 normally marks un-synapsed chromosomes (including sex chromosomes).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HORMAD1 function.

claim: HORMAD1 is removed by TRIP13 on synapsis.
source: While HORMAD1 is removed by TRIP13 on synapsis, it persists on asynapsed chromosomes, which then undergo MSUC, leading to MSCI for the sex chromosomes (Shin et al., 2010; Wojtasz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shin et al., 2010 and Wojtasz et al., 2009.

claim: In Hormad1-/- spermatocytes, double-strand break formation and early recombination are disrupted as marked by the reduction of yH2AX, DMC1, and RAD51 foci.
source: In Hormad1-/- spermatocytes, double-strand break formation and early recombination are disrupted as marked by the reduction of yH2AX, DMC1, and RAD51 foci (Shin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shin et al., 2010.

claim: Hormad1-/- mutant cells experience apoptosis during meiosis I due to pachytene checkpoint failure.
source: Hard clustering analysis (Figure 1F & G) showed a deficit of post-pachytene Hormad1-/- germ cells, consistent with the expectation that Hormad1-/- mutant cells experience apoptosis during meiosis I due to pachytene checkpoint failure (Daniel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on analysis of cell type composition shown in Figure 1F & G and supported by a citation to Daniel et al., 2011.

claim: Hormad1-/- leptotene/zygotene cells form a distinct cluster outside of the leptotene/zygotene cells of all other strains.
source: Along with this arrest phenotype, the Hormad1-/- leptotene/zygotene cells form a distinct cluster outside of the leptotene/zygotene cells of all other strains (Cluster 30, Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: CUL4A is a major component of the E3 ubiquitin ligase complex called CRL4.
source: CUL4A is a major component of the E3 ubiquitin ligase complex called CRL4 which is known to regulate cell cycle, DNA replication, DNA repair, and chromatin remodeling (Dubiel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dubiel et al., 2018.

claim: In Cul4a-/- mice, some spermatocytes arrest at the pachytene stage of meiosis I induced by the pachytene checkpoint, whereas remaining spermatocytes complete meiosis but the resulting spermatozoa present oligoasthenospermia and severe malformations.
source: Studies on Cul4a-/- mice noted that some spermatocytes arrest at the pachytene stage of meiosis I induced by the pachytene checkpoint, whereas remaining spermatocytes complete meiosis but the resulting spermatozoa present oligoasthenospermia and severe malformations (Yin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yin et al., 2011.

claim: MLH3 is an essential protein required for crossover formation in early meiosis and for binding of MLH1 to meiotic chromosomes.

claim: SDA revealed previously uncharacterized complexity, with multiple different components even within recognised meiotic stages such as pachytene.

This revealed previously uncharacterized complexity, with multiple different components even within recognised meiotic stages such as pachytene.
evidence: This is based on the SDA analysis results.
